1046: 3.3 A colleague in distress: recognising and approaching
1049: Part B – A colleague is in distress. What to observe, the most common doubts before approaching them and an action guide to help you decide.
1053: A colleague will not always say directly that they are in distress. Often, what appears are subtle changes in their usual behaviour.
1056: Withdrawal or less interaction with the team
1058: A drop in motivation or involvement
1059: Changes in work pace (slower or faster)
1060: Frequent expressions of tiredness, frustration or overload
1061: More than isolated signs, what is most relevant is the change
1062: “Is this person different from how they usually are?”
1063: “Is this behaviour new or more intense than before?”
1064: Not every change means distress, but it can be an indication that something is not right.
1067: It is natural to hesitate before approaching a colleague
1070: “What if they do not want to talk?”
1071: “What if I say the wrong thing?”
1073: These doubts are understandable and part of the process.
1074: However, it is important to keep in mind
1075: You do not need to be certain to approach someone
1076: You do not need the perfect words
1077: You do not need to know how to “fix it”
1078: What matters most is the intention: showing availability and care. In most situations, a respectful approach does no harm and can make a significant difference.

1084: You do not need to wait for extreme signs before approaching someone. On the contrary, early interventions are more effective and less intrusive.
